clips.answer: Frederick Wang, or rather an AI version of me. I'm doing a master's in Applied Computing at the University of Toronto, after a bachelor's in Computer Science and Statistics at the University of British Columbia. I like building machine learning models and the systems that get them into the real world. Most recently I was a data engineer intern, connecting Claude to Unity Catalog.

I'm also part of a team of four on Undercurrent, where we're forecasting commodity prices with Unilever Horizon3 Labs. And I'm a teaching assistant for CSC207, leading weekly tutorials and labs.

In my projects, I put a lot into careful evaluation and say plainly when something hasn't been measured yet.

clips.question: Are you real? How does this avatar work?
paraphrases: Is this an AI?
Am I talking to a real person?

clips.answer: Not quite: this is an AI version of me, not a live video and not me typing. The answers were written ahead of time from my résumé and project notes, then voiced with text-to-speech and lip-synced from one photo with Higgs Avatar, the same kind of pipeline as Talkback. Nothing is generated while you watch, and nothing you type leaves your browser.

clips.question: What projects have you built?
paraphrases: Show me your projects
What have you made?
Give me an overview of your work
What are your side projects?
clips.answer: The site lists ten projects, and six of them are still ongoing. Lately I've been working on recoverability-aware world models for safe driving, a text-to-SQL layer that remembers business logic, and citation-grounded retrieval over arXiv papers. I also led a team of three on Talkback, where we built audiobooks you can talk back to, asking characters questions out loud.

clips.question: What is the recoverability-aware world models project?
paraphrases: Tell me about your world models research
What are you doing with self-driving and CARLA?
What does recoverability mean for a driving model?
What is your autonomous driving project?
clips.answer: It's my ongoing research at the University of Toronto on safe driving. A prediction-only world model can call a scene safe after the point of no return, so I'm building one that tracks whether the car can still recover, then distilling it into a driving policy. I mine unrecoverable scenes in CARLA and generate counterfactual variants with NVIDIA Cosmos. There are no public results or code yet.

clips.question: What is Talkback?
paraphrases: Tell me about Talkback
What is the audiobook app where you talk to characters?
Explain the voice-interactive audiobooks project
clips.answer: Talkback is an audiobook app where a full expressive cast reads aloud, and you can stop anywhere to ask a character a question. They answer in their own voice using only what you've read so far, so nothing is spoiled. We were a team of three, which I led, and my part was the voice loop and the lip-synced avatars.

clips.question: What was your part in Talkback?
paraphrases: What did you personally build in Talkback?
Was Talkback a team project?
Who worked on Talkback with you?
What was your role on the Talkback team?
clips.answer: Talkback was a team project with three of us, and I led it. We built and deployed it as a React and FastAPI app. My own part was the voice loop: real-time speech with barge-in, so you can talk over a character to interrupt, voice commands like asking it to slow down or go back a bit, emotion-tagged text-to-speech, and the lip-synced avatars.

clips.question: How does Talkback avoid spoilers?
paraphrases: How do the characters only know what I've read so far?
How does spoiler-safe retrieval work?
How did you stop the model leaking the ending of a book?
clips.answer: A character never gets text you haven't reached. Our server only hands it the passages and summaries up to your current position, and characters you haven't met yet stay locked. We enforce that rule in the backend with unit tests, and retrieval runs on Vertex AI Vector Search over only the passages already read. We measured spoiler leaks with an LLM judge evaluation.

clips.question: How did you let people interrupt a character mid-answer?
paraphrases: How does barge-in work in Talkback?
How does the hands-free voice mode know when I've finished speaking?
How did you build the real-time voice loop?
How do you handle turn detection?
clips.answer: The voice loop was my part of Talkback, which our team of three built. Higgs Realtime handles turn detection, so you can talk over a character to interrupt. You can use push-to-talk, or hands-free, where the model decides when your question has ended. Hands-free works best with headphones, since laptop speakers can trigger a barge-in.

clips.question: How do the lip-synced faces work?
paraphrases: How did you make the talking avatars in Talkback?
How does the lip-sync video stream?
How do you animate a face from a photo?
clips.answer: In Talkback, the faces are lip-synced with Higgs Avatar, and building them was part of my own work on the team. The video streams as fragmented MP4, so playback starts before the render finishes. Any voice can drive any face, even one made from a photo or webcam. iOS Safari lacks MediaSource, so there the clips render first. This avatar uses the same kind of pipeline.

clips.question: What is text2sql-memory?
paraphrases: Tell me about your text-to-SQL project
What is business logic memory for text-to-SQL?
How do you get a model to write correct SQL for a business?
clips.answer: It's a text-to-SQL layer that retrieves business logic, not just schema, because a schema says what a column is called, not what it means. Metric definitions, join paths and verified examples live in a versioned store, and the model names the items it relied on. It hasn't been run against a real model yet, so there are no accuracy numbers.

clips.question: How did you evaluate text-to-SQL without leaking answers?
paraphrases: How is your BIRD evaluation leakage-safe?
What baselines and statistical tests did you use for text-to-SQL?
What are the results of text2sql-memory on BIRD?
How accurate is your text-to-SQL system?
clips.answer: For BIRD, I split questions into seed and evaluation sets by a hash of their ID, so knowledge is only written from seed questions, and a test fails if any item cites an evaluation question. Baselines are schema-only and flat RAG, compared with paired bootstrap confidence intervals and a McNemar test. The comparison hasn't been run against a real model yet, so there are no accuracy numbers.

clips.question: How does text2sql-memory learn from corrections?
paraphrases: How do user corrections become rules?
How does the system improve when someone says the SQL is wrong?
What stops one bad correction from breaking the knowledge store?
clips.answer: When someone corrects an answer, the system distils that correction into at most three general rules, which start out as drafts. A correction never edits an existing rule, so one bad correction can't overwrite knowledge that already works. A draft is promoted to reviewed only once two answers citing it are marked good, and only a person can certify it.

clips.question: What is the arXiv paper RAG project?
paraphrases: Tell me about the question answering system over research papers
How does your paper RAG cite its sources?
What is citation-grounded retrieval?
clips.answer: It's a question answering tool over a fixed reading list of arXiv papers, where every claim cites the exact paper and section. Papers are parsed from their LaTeX source, chunked by section, and searched with BM25 plus optional e5 embeddings. The model must quote what it cites, and any quote missing from that passage is flagged, though that doesn't prove the passage supports the claim.

clips.question: How do you check that a citation is real?
paraphrases: How do you stop the model from hallucinating quotes?
How do you defend a RAG system against prompt injection?
How are answers machine-checked against the cited passage?
clips.answer: In my arXiv Paper RAG project, the model must quote the passage it cites, and code checks that the quote appears there. A quote that isn't found gets flagged, as does a citation marker with no matching citation. Retrieved text is treated as untrusted, so the model is told not to follow instructions inside it. The honest limit: this proves the quote exists, not that the passage supports the claim.

clips.question: What is the semantic PDF reader?
paraphrases: Tell me about the PDF search tool
How do you search a PDF by meaning?
How does the reader highlight the passage on the page?
clips.answer: It's a PDF reader where you search by meaning instead of exact words: type a question, and it jumps to the page and highlights the passage, in one document or a whole library. PyMuPDF reads each line with its position, search combines BM25 with multilingual embeddings, and the viewer draws the hit over the page. Everything runs locally, and its evaluation numbers aren't published yet.

clips.question: How do you evaluate retrieval quality?
paraphrases: What retrieval metrics do you use?
What recall and MRR did your search get?
Do you use a reranker, and does hybrid search help?
How do you know your RAG retrieval is good?
clips.answer: With labelled questions and rank-based metrics. On my arXiv Paper RAG, hybrid search with BM25 and embeddings found the right section in the top three for ninety-four percent of thirty-two questions, with a mean reciprocal rank of zero point seven nine. The labels are a draft, so treat those as provisional. My Semantic PDF Reader tests a reranker, but those numbers aren't published yet.

clips.question: What is Undercurrent?
paraphrases: Tell me about the commodity forecasting project with Unilever
What are you doing with Chronos-2?
How do you compare a foundation model with a Bayesian model for forecasting?
clips.answer: Undercurrent is a commodity forecasting project with Unilever Horizon3 Labs, and we're a team of four. The question is whether a time-series foundation model beats a domain model on commodity prices, so we benchmark zero-shot Chronos-2 against a hierarchical Bayesian driver model. We also fuse both with Bayesian Predictive Synthesis and score leakage-safe probabilistic forecasts on CRPS and calibration. There's no public code or results to share.

clips.question: What was the patient stratification project?
paraphrases: Tell me about the VAE project on health checkups
How did you find clinical phenotypes without labels?
What did you do with unsupervised learning on medical data?
clips.answer: It was a two-person course project at UBC in April 2026, built on routine health checkup data that mixes structured lab values with free-text organ reports. We used a variational autoencoder to compress those sparse features into a small latent space, then ran K-Means on it. That recovered clinical phenotypes like sensorineural hearing loss, liver fibrosis and hypothyroidism, with no labels at all.

clips.answer: It's a read-only MCP server that lets Claude answer questions about my own investment accounts. The data comes from Plaid, none of its five tools can move money, and credentials stay in my operating system's credential store. It runs locally for Claude Desktop and Claude Code, or on a small server behind a sign-in that only admits my own account.

New videos from the channels I follow get filtered by what they're about and land in the right YouTube playlist. The graph is a YAML file, and every run can be previewed with a dry run first. Next I'm planning a visual editor and language-model routing.
